conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived, not to judge or label you in any way. We’ll use a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s just 10 gentle questions about the past seven days; it helps us see if you might benefit from a little extra support or simply a listening ear. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the small team who may help with your care. When you’re ready, I’ll ask the questions conversationally—no need to remember any numbers—and we’ll go at your pace. Shall we begin?

Over the past week, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly… most of the time I can still laugh if something’s genuinely funny, but it feels like it takes more effort than it used to. Like, I’ll smile or chuckle, but it doesn’t come as easily or feel as light-hearted as before I had the baby.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… I can still laugh, but it’s not the same. It feels kind of forced sometimes, like I have to remind myself to enjoy the moment instead of just naturally feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some small things—like my husband coming home so I’m not alone with the baby, or the neighbor dropping off a coffee—but the bigger “fun” stuff I used to plan doesn’t excite me much right now. I’ll think “that’ll be nice,” yet I don’t feel the little spark I used to get.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like if the baby won’t settle, I catch myself thinking, “What am I doing wrong?” even when people tell me it’s normal. It’s not every time—just every now and then I get that little pang of “this is my fault.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

It happens. Most of the worry is about the baby—like, is he breathing okay, is he eating enough—but sometimes the anxious feeling just sits there even when everything looks fine. It’s not constant, but it pops up a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky, more like a sudden knot in my stomach—like when the baby’s asleep and the house is quiet, I’ll get this flash that something bad could happen even though nothing’s wrong. It passes quickly, but it’s unsettling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… some days it feels like the feedings, the laundry, the never-ending “to-do” list all pile up. I manage, but by late afternoon I’m worn out and thinking, “How am I going to keep doing this tomorrow?” It’s not hopeless, just… heavy.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I’m tired, but when I finally lie down my mind keeps ticking—mostly running through baby stuff or little worries—so it takes me a while to fall asleep. I wouldn’t say I’m so unhappy I can’t sleep; it’s more that I can’t shut my brain off.
I have felt sad or miserable
I do feel sad some of the time, maybe a couple of days this week. It’s not there all day—comes in waves, usually when I’m alone with the baby and everything feels quiet and endless.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I got a little teary one evening when my husband asked how my day was, but actual crying—no, I haven’t broken down or anything.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I’ve felt overwhelmed, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression Screening Summary  
Date: [today]

Source of data: Patient self-report on 10-item postpartum screening questionnaire.

Symptoms endorsed:
- Diminished ability to enjoy or look forward to activities (Q1, Q2)
- Intermittent sadness, “waves” of low mood (Q8)
- Mild, situational guilt/blaming self when baby fussy (Q3)
- Generalized worry and “knot-in-stomach” anxiety without clear trigger (Q4, Q5)
- Feeling overwhelmed by daily tasks; end-of-day fatigue (Q6)
- Sleep-onset difficulty secondary to racing thoughts (Q7)

Symptoms denied:
- Frequent crying episodes (Q9)
- Panic attacks (Q5)
- Self-harm ideation (Q10)

Pattern: Sub-syndromal depressive and anxiety symptoms beginning post-delivery, waxing and waning, most prominent during solitary infant care. No safety concerns identified at this time.

Screening significance: Meets partial criteria for Perinatal Depression and Anxiety; score suggests moderate distress that warrants closer monitoring and possible referral for formal evaluation.

Risk factors noted:
- Loss of pleasure/anhedonia
- Mood-linked insomnia
- Recurrent “what if” worries about infant safety
- Absence of suicidal ideation

Plan: Provide psycho-education, encourage supports, recommend follow-up within 1–2 weeks or sooner if symptoms worsen; consider standardized EPDS for quantification and referral to perinatal mental health specialist as indicated.
